title: Aggregating & Grouping Data
description: Summarize rows into numbers with COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX, group them with GROUP BY, and filter groups with HAVING

lessons.title: Aggregate Functions
lessons.description: Turn many rows into one summary number with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX to summarize a whole column into a single value.

sections.title: 📊 From many rows to one number
sections.content:
So far every query has returned a list of rows. **Aggregate functions** do the opposite — they collapse a whole column down into a single summary value.

**The five you'll use constantly:**
• `COUNT(*)` — how many rows
• `SUM(column)` — total of a numeric column
• `AVG(column)` — average of a numeric column
• `MIN(column)` / `MAX(column)` — smallest / largest value

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
       SUM(total_amount) AS revenue,
       AVG(total_amount) AS avg_order_value
FROM orders;
```

This returns exactly **one row** — the whole table boiled down to three numbers.

sections.title: 🔢 COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)
sections.content:
These look similar but answer different questions:

• `COUNT(*)` counts every row, no matter what's in it
• `COUNT(column)` counts only rows where that column is **not NULL**

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_employees,
       COUNT(manager_id) AS employees_with_a_manager
FROM employees;
```

If some employees have no manager (manager_id is NULL), the two numbers will differ — and that difference itself is useful information.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Mixing an aggregate function with a plain column in the same SELECT without GROUP BY (covered next lesson) — most databases will reject this or give a confusing result. Assuming AVG ignores NULLs the way you'd expect without checking — it does skip NULLs, but it's worth confirming for the database you're using.

questions.question: What does SUM(total_amount) return when run over the whole orders table?
options: One row per order, showing its amount
A single number: the total of all total_amount values
The largest total_amount value
The number of orders
questions.explanation: SUM adds up every value in the column across all matching rows and returns one total.

questions.question: If manager_id is NULL for some employees, what's true about COUNT(*) vs COUNT(manager_id)?
options: They always return the same number
COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(manager_id) skips rows where manager_id is NULL, so it can be smaller
COUNT(manager_id) always errors on NULL values
COUNT(*) only counts rows where every column is non-NULL
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of content. COUNT(column) only counts rows where that specific column has a non-NULL value.

questions.question: Which function would you use to find the single most expensive product in the products table?
options: AVG(price)
COUNT(price)
MAX(price)
SUM(price)
questions.explanation: MAX(price) returns the largest value in the price column across all rows — exactly the most expensive product's price.

questions.question: What does the AVG() function calculate?
options: The average (mean) of a numeric column across matching rows
The total count of rows
The largest value in a column
The smallest value in a column
questions.explanation: AVG() computes the mean of the values in the specified column.

questions.question: What does COUNT(*) count?
options: The total number of rows, regardless of NULLs in any column
Only rows where every column is non-NULL
The number of columns in the table
The number of distinct values in the table
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows themselves, not values in a specific column, so NULLs don't exclude a row.

questions.question: What does MIN(price) return?
options: The smallest price value among matching rows
The largest price value
The average price
The number of distinct prices
questions.explanation: MIN() finds the smallest value in the specified column.

questions.question: Can aggregate functions like SUM() and AVG() be used together in one SELECT?
options: Yes, you can compute multiple aggregates in the same query
No, only one aggregate function is allowed per query
Only if the table has fewer than 100 rows
Only if GROUP BY is omitted
questions.explanation: Multiple aggregate functions can appear together in a single SELECT statement.

questions.question: What does SUM(quantity) return if the quantity column has some NULL values?
options: NULLs are ignored, and non-NULL quantities are summed
The whole query fails with an error
NULL values count as zero automatically breaking the sum
SUM() cannot be used on any column containing NULLs
questions.explanation: Aggregate functions like SUM() skip NULL values rather than erroring or miscounting.

lessons.title: Grouping Rows with GROUP BY
lessons.description: Get one summary row per category instead of one for the whole table

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Use GROUP BY to compute an aggregate per category instead of over the whole table.

sections.title: 🗂️ One summary per group
sections.content:
Aggregate functions alone collapse the *entire* table into one row. `GROUP BY` changes that: it collapses the table into **one row per distinct value** of a column.

```sql
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count, AVG(price) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category;
```

This answers "for each category, how many products and what's the average price?" — instead of one number for the whole store, you get one row per category.

sections.title: 🧩 The rule: every non-aggregated column must be grouped
sections.content:
Any column in `SELECT` that isn't wrapped in an aggregate function **must** appear in `GROUP BY` — otherwise the database wouldn't know which value to show for that group.

```sql
-- Works: category is grouped, product_count is aggregated
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count
FROM products
GROUP BY category;

-- Fails: name isn't grouped and isn't aggregated either
SELECT category, name, COUNT(*)
FROM products
GROUP BY category;
```

You can group by more than one column too — `GROUP BY category, city` gives one row per unique **combination** of category and city.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to add a column to GROUP BY when it's also in SELECT. Grouping by a column you don't actually need in the output, which multiplies the number of result rows unexpectedly. Expecting the output rows to be in a particular order — add ORDER BY if it matters.

questions.question: What does GROUP BY category do to a products query?
options: Sorts products alphabetically by category
Collapses the results into one row per distinct category value
Removes the category column from the output
Filters out products with no category
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows sharing the same value in the grouped column(s) into a single summary row per group.

questions.question: Why does SELECT category, name, COUNT(*) FROM products GROUP BY category; usually fail?
options: COUNT(*) can't be used with GROUP BY
name is neither aggregated nor included in GROUP BY, so the database doesn't know which name to show per group
category must always be aggregated
GROUP BY requires exactly one column in SELECT
questions.explanation: Every selected column that isn't inside an aggregate function must appear in GROUP BY — otherwise there could be many different name values within one category group, and SQL won't guess which to show.

questions.question: What does GROUP BY category, city produce?
options: One row per category only
One row per city only
One row for each unique combination of category and city
An error, since GROUP BY only accepts one column
questions.explanation: Grouping by multiple columns produces one row per unique combination of those columns' values.

questions.question: What must every non-aggregated column in a SELECT be, when GROUP BY is used?
options: Listed in the GROUP BY clause
Wrapped in a COUNT() function
Removed from the SELECT entirely
Placed only in the WHERE clause
questions.explanation: Any column that's not inside an aggregate function must appear in GROUP BY, or the query is invalid in standard SQL.

questions.question: What does `GROUP BY category` produce, when paired with COUNT(*)?
options: One row per distinct category, with a count of rows in that category
One row per original row in the table
A single row summing the whole table
An error, since GROUP BY needs no aggregate
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows sharing the same category value into one summary row per category.

questions.question: Can you GROUP BY more than one column at once?
options: Yes, grouping by multiple columns creates one row per unique combination of those columns
No, GROUP BY only accepts a single column
Only if the columns are the same data type
Only in combination with ORDER BY
questions.explanation: Multiple columns in GROUP BY create groups based on the combination of all listed columns.

questions.question: What happens to rows with a NULL value in the GROUP BY column?
options: They form their own group of NULLs
They are silently dropped from the results
They cause the whole query to fail
They are merged into a random existing group
questions.explanation: SQL treats NULL as its own group value for grouping purposes, rather than excluding those rows.

questions.question: Does the order of columns in GROUP BY need to match the order in SELECT?
options: No, but the same columns still need to appear in both
Yes, they must be in the exact same order
GROUP BY columns can never overlap with SELECT columns
Order never matters for any part of a SQL query
questions.explanation: The columns need to be consistent between SELECT and GROUP BY, but their listed order relative to each other isn't required to match.

lessons.title: Filtering Groups with HAVING
lessons.description: Filter on the aggregated result, not the raw rows

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and use HAVING to filter grouped/aggregated results.

sections.title: 🚧 Why WHERE isn't enough
sections.content:
`WHERE` filters rows **before** grouping happens — so it can't reference an aggregate like COUNT(*) or AVG(price), because those don't exist yet at that point. `HAVING` filters **after** grouping, on the aggregated results:

```sql
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
```

This finds categories with **more than 5 products** — a question that only makes sense after grouping.

sections.title: 🔀 Using WHERE and HAVING together
sections.content:
They aren't mutually exclusive — most real queries use both, because they filter at different stages:

```sql
SELECT category, AVG(price) AS avg_price
FROM products
WHERE stock_qty > 0            -- filter rows first: only in-stock items
GROUP BY category
HAVING AVG(price) > 20;        -- then filter the grouped result
```

**The order to remember:** `WHERE` (raw rows) → `GROUP BY` (form groups) → `HAVING` (filter groups).

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Trying to use an aggregate function inside WHERE — it belongs in HAVING instead. Using HAVING for a filter that doesn't involve an aggregate — that filter should be in WHERE, since it's simpler and faster there.

questions.question: What's the key difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: They're interchangeable and always do the same thing
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
HAVING only works with SELECT *
WHERE can only be used with numbers, HAVING only with text
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY runs. HAVING filters the resulting groups, so it can reference aggregate functions like COUNT() or AVG().

questions.question: Which clause would you use to find categories with an average price above 20?
options: WHERE AVG(price) > 20
HAVING AVG(price) > 20
GROUP BY AVG(price) > 20
ORDER BY AVG(price) > 20
questions.explanation: AVG(price) only exists after grouping, so filtering on it requires HAVING, not WHERE.

questions.question: In a query with WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING all present, what order do they logically apply in?
options: HAVING, then GROUP BY, then WHERE
GROUP BY, then WHERE, then HAVING
WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING
They all apply at the same time
questions.explanation: SQL first filters raw rows with WHERE, then forms groups with GROUP BY, then filters those groups with HAVING.

questions.question: Can HAVING reference an aggregate function like SUM() or COUNT()?
options: Yes, that's exactly what HAVING is designed for
No, aggregates can only appear in SELECT
Only if WHERE is also present
Only for COUNT(), never SUM() or AVG()
questions.explanation: HAVING filters based on the result of aggregate functions, which WHERE cannot do.

questions.question: Can a query use both WHERE and HAVING together?
options: Yes — WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after
No, only one of them can appear in a query
Only if GROUP BY is omitted
WHERE and HAVING always do the exact same thing
questions.explanation: WHERE and HAVING operate at different stages and are commonly used together.

questions.question: What happens if you try to use an aggregate function like COUNT() inside a WHERE clause?
options: It causes an error, since WHERE runs before aggregation happens
It works exactly like it would in HAVING
It automatically converts to a HAVING clause
It only works with COUNT(), never other aggregates
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping or aggregation occurs, so aggregate functions aren't valid there.

questions.question: If you omit HAVING from a query with GROUP BY, what happens?
options: All groups are returned, with no group-level filtering applied
The query returns zero rows
GROUP BY stops working entirely
The query defaults to filtering out empty groups only
questions.explanation: HAVING is optional — without it, every group produced by GROUP BY appears in the result.

questions.question: Can HAVING filter on a column that isn't an aggregate?
options: Yes, as long as that column is also in the GROUP BY
No, HAVING can only reference aggregate functions
Only if the column is a primary key
Only when WHERE is also used
questions.explanation: HAVING can reference grouped (non-aggregate) columns too, not just aggregate expressions.

lessons.title: Putting It Together: A Sales Report
lessons.description: Combine WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, and ORDER BY into one real report query

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write a single query that filters, groups, aggregates, filters again, and sorts — the shape of a typical real-world report.

sections.title: 📈 A realistic question
sections.content:
"Which customers spent more than $200 in total, ranked from highest spender down?" This single question needs everything from this module at once:

```sql
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*)         AS order_count,
       SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent
FROM orders
WHERE status != 'cancelled'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(total_amount) > 200
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
```

Read it top to bottom and it tells a story: start from orders, ignore cancelled ones, group by customer, keep only the big spenders, and show the biggest first.

sections.title: 🧠 The mental checklist for any report query
sections.content:
When a question feels complicated, break it into these steps in order:

• Which table has the raw data? (`FROM`)
• Do I need to exclude some rows before summarizing? (`WHERE`)
• What am I summarizing *by*? (`GROUP BY`)
• What am I measuring for each group? (aggregate functions in `SELECT`)
• Do I only want groups that meet some condition? (`HAVING`)
• How should the final list be ordered? (`ORDER BY`)

Almost every real reporting query is built from this same six-step shape — SQL just gives you clauses for each step.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Writing HAVING before GROUP BY in the query (SQL requires this exact clause order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY). Forgetting ORDER BY and assuming the biggest spender is already at the top.

questions.question: In standard SQL clause order, which comes first: GROUP BY or HAVING?
options: HAVING always comes first
GROUP BY comes first, then HAVING
They must be written on the same line
Order doesn't matter
questions.explanation: SQL clauses must appear in this order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY. GROUP BY forms the groups before HAVING can filter them.

questions.question: In the report query above, what does WHERE status != 'cancelled' accomplish?
options: Removes cancelled orders before they're included in any customer's total
Removes customers who have ever cancelled an order
Sorts cancelled orders to the bottom
Has no effect since HAVING would filter them anyway
questions.explanation: WHERE filters raw order rows before grouping, so cancelled orders never contribute to a customer's order_count or total_spent in the first place.

questions.question: What does HAVING SUM(total_amount) > 200 keep in the final result?
options: Only individual orders over $200
Only customers whose combined order total exceeds $200
Only orders placed after $200 was spent
Nothing — HAVING can't reference SUM
questions.explanation: Because grouping is by customer_id, SUM(total_amount) is each customer's total spend, and HAVING keeps only the groups (customers) where that total exceeds $200.

questions.question: In a query combining WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING, which clause runs conceptually first?
options: WHERE, filtering raw rows before grouping happens
HAVING, filtering before any grouping
GROUP BY, before WHERE is even considered
They all run simultaneously with no order
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows first; then GROUP BY forms groups; then HAVING filters those groups.

questions.question: Why might a sales report query need both a WHERE and a HAVING clause?
options: To exclude certain raw rows (WHERE) and then also exclude certain resulting groups (HAVING)
Because WHERE and HAVING must always appear together
Because GROUP BY requires two filtering clauses to function
Because one clause is required for each aggregate function used
questions.explanation: WHERE and HAVING serve different filtering purposes — row-level versus group-level — which is exactly why a report might need both.

questions.question: What would `ORDER BY SUM(total_amount) DESC` do at the end of a grouped report query?
options: Sort the grouped results by their total spending, highest first
Sort by the number of groups produced
Cause an error since ORDER BY can't use aggregates
Sort alphabetically by category name instead
questions.explanation: ORDER BY can reference an aggregate expression to sort the final grouped rows by that computed value.

questions.question: If a sales report groups by customer_id, what does each row in the result represent?
options: A summary of all of one customer's orders
A single individual order
A single product
The entire company's total sales
questions.explanation: Grouping by customer_id collapses every order for that customer into one summary row.

questions.question: Why is it good practice to alias an aggregate column, like `SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent`?
options: It gives the computed column a clear, readable name in the result set
It changes how the SUM is calculated
It's required for GROUP BY to function at all
It converts the aggregate into a filter automatically
questions.explanation: Aliasing makes the output more readable and gives you a name to reference elsewhere, like in ORDER BY.
